prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable measurement of frequency with unprecedented precision

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement advance of the kind that changes what physics can observe. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift that would otherwise ruin spectroscopy of trapped atoms, and it lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed. Ye's group then took the accuracy and stability to the 10^-18 level and demonstrated the many-body coherence that underlies it. The result is reproduced and compared across independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others), which for an experimentalist is the decisive test of a claim. It has opened relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, tests of constant variation and dark-matter searches, and it underpins the coming redefinition of the second. Four of eight members placed it first, and the support comes from members with different specialties, which makes me trust it more than a candidate favoured only by its own subfield. The credit is a clean pair, with no three-person squeeze and no missing principal.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with prior metrology prizes: the frequency comb (2005) and ion-trap clocks and quantum control (2012) already honour much of the surrounding toolbox, so a committee could call the lattice clock an incremental refinement of recognised ideas. A second concern is that the headline numbers (10^-18) and the redefinition of the second are still moving, so part of the practical payoff lies ahead. Others besides the two names, such as Lemonde, Derevianko and the early NIST and PTB groups, helped mature the concept, and I have not verified every priority detail.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the lattice clock only fifth and notes that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-clock prize may reduce its novelty, while his first choice is the topological insulator story (B004).
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously but disagree on its weight. The comb is the ruler that counts optical cycles, and the Wineland ion clock is a different physical system with one ion and large quantum-projection noise. The lattice clock's contribution is the magic-wavelength condition and the resulting shift from one ion to a huge ensemble, which is what gave the order-of-magnitude gain in stability and the access to geodesy and many-body clock physics. A citation worded around the lattice and magic wavelength separates it cleanly. I also agree with Danielsson that B004 is conceptually deep, but I cannot judge it as a measurement and I note that his own assessment says no clean three-person set exists within the supplied names (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang), which is a real problem for a prize.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B041 first because the magic-wavelength idea fits the close link between atomic structure, laser control and measurement, and because 10^-18 agreement has been reproduced internationally.
responses.response: I agree and add the experimental caveat that makes the case stronger, not weaker: the 10^-18 level is not a single group's claim but rests on systematic-shift budgets (blackbody radiation, lattice light shifts, collisions) checked by clock comparisons between laboratories. Her point that Hall and Hänsch were already honoured for the comb is the right framing for the citation. Where I would push back slightly is on B034 (atom interferometry), which she ranks fifth and I rank second: she is right that the credit there is messy, with Chu absent and Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich overlapping, and I accept that this makes it a weaker lead candidate than the clocks.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B041 first as a new measurement technique, but places IceCube (B029) second and gamma-ray burst afterglows (B011) third, valuing the instrument-driven discoveries.
responses.response: I share his preference for instruments that create a new window, and IceCube is a serious alternative. My concern is the one he himself raises: the credit inside a roughly 300-person collaboration is hard to pin to two or three names, and TXS 0506+056 sits near 3 sigma while the Galactic-plane and NGC 1068 results are newer. The clock has no such attribution problem. On B011 I would add that without van Paradijs the credit looks incomplete, so I would not put it above the clock. Pearce's willingness to rely on AMO colleagues for attribution is fine, and on that I can state that the Katori and Ye pairing is the defensible one.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B041 only sixth after KTHNY melting (B027), is unsure how the committee weighs metrology against discovery of a new phenomenon, and notes Ye also appears in another candidate.
responses.response: On weighting, measurement achievements have been rewarded when they open a new regime, and here the new regime is concrete: clocks that resolve a gravitational redshift over millimetres and make fundamental constants testable at a new level. That is both a measurement and a discovery tool. I accept that KTHNY melting is an elegant mechanism, but I see a real risk that the 2016 recognition of topological defects is judged to have covered its central insight, as he himself flags, and its experimental tests in real 2D systems are not uniform. Ye appearing elsewhere is not a reason to withhold the prize from the clock itself.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B028) first as a clean, foundational platform that follows the 2025 prize, while placing the lattice clock fourth, deferring to atomic physics colleagues on priority.
responses.response: I appreciate the deference and will supply the AMO judgment he asks for: the lattice clock priority is clear and the pair is well defined. On circuit QED I fully agree it is foundational, and I ranked it fifth, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits and the four-name credit problem with Blais left out make it a harder prize to set this year. He has also flagged his own closeness to the community, which should be handled by recusal for that candidate, and I would count his opening support for B028 accordingly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly to separate it from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether other early proposers or demonstrators of lattice clocks deserve credit beyond Katori and Ye; I have not independently verified the priority chronology.
The latest 10^-18 accuracy figures and the status of the redefinition of the second were not checked against sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B041. As a minor note, during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's group is part of the broader JILA environment in which Ye works; this was a visit and not a collaboration with either candidate, and I do not consider it grounds for recusal. I am not connected to any other shortlisted candidate, though my WACQT role touches the Chalmers community relevant to B028.
